title: Concrete Contractor Software: Bids, Pours and Crew Tools
html:
Concrete contractor software has to cover four jobs: measure, bid, schedule the pour and bill. Use a takeoff tool such as STACK, a project tool such as JobTread and a scheduler such as Jobber. Add a website that brings in bid requests. Published plans in this guide run from $0 to $299 a month.

Concrete contractor software earns its price on the bid. A flatwork or foundation bid depends on square feet, thickness, rebar, forms and finishing, and one wrong number eats the margin. The right tool measures once, prices from a saved cost list and carries the numbers into the job.

This guide sorts tools by the step in the job where they help: takeoff and bidding, project control, scheduling, photos and books. Each tool shows the price its own vendor lists and one real limit.

Which concrete contractor software handles takeoffs and bids?

STACK is the clearest takeoff and estimating product on this list, and Contractor Foreman and JobTread add estimating inside a wider project system. Pick by how many bids you write each month.

A takeoff tool pays back when you bid often enough to repeat the same slab, footing and wall shapes. If you write three bids a month from a tape and a calculator, a free tier and a good spreadsheet may be enough. If you write thirty, a paid takeoff seat is cheap next to one missed rebar line.

Save your own unit costs before you bid in any tool. Concrete price per yard, finishing labor per square foot and pump fees change by market. Store them as a price list in the software, and update it every quarter so old numbers do not leak into new bids.

Which software schedules pours and crews?

Pour days are weather days, and a good scheduler makes rescheduling painless. Jobber and ServiceM8 are two scheduling apps priced for small trade crews.

  • Jobber: Core is $49 a month with no commitment or $29 a month billed annually, for one user. Connect starts at $139 a month for one user with no commitment. Extra users cost $29 a month each. Limit: card payments cost 2.9% plus 30 cents, which matters on large invoices.
  • ServiceM8: Free is $0 for 1 user and 30 jobs a month. Starter is $29 for 50 jobs, Growing is $79 for 150 jobs and Premium is $149 for 500 jobs, with unlimited users on paid plans. Limit: each plan caps jobs per month.

Ask how each tool handles a rainout. A good one lets you drag a pour to a new day and texts the homeowner or general contractor in one step. A weak one makes you edit each job by hand, which costs an hour on a bad forecast week.

Remember that a pour is rarely one visit, and that forms, steel inspection and finishing all take crew days. Forming, inspection, pour and finishing may be four separate stops. Decide whether your plan counts each as a job, because per-job caps on plans such as ServiceM8 count every stop.

What do small concrete crews use for estimates and invoices?

A small flatwork or decorative crew may not need project software at all. Joist sends estimates and invoices and takes online payments.

  • Joist: Basics is $10 a month and Pro is $17 a month on monthly billing. Elite is $32 and Run is $100. Limit: Basics allows 5 documents a month, which a busy crew passes in a week.

This fits a driveway and patio crew that quotes by the square foot. Build a template per product: broom finish, stamped, exposed aggregate, footings. A signed estimate with a deposit protects you from ordering concrete for a job that falls through. Joist stores each estimate and invoice, so you can see what a customer approved before the truck is booked. Keep decorative and structural work on separate templates, because their risks and margins differ.

Which tools keep job photos and the books in order?

Two small tools close the loop: a photo app for proof of work and an accounting package for the books.

  • CompanyCam: stores timestamped photos by project. Core is $63 a month billed annually, Crew is $129 and Scale is $199, with extra users at $29. Limit: Core includes one user and caps at two.
  • QuickBooks Online: Simple Start is $19 a month for the first three months, then $38. Essentials is $42.50, then $85, and Plus is $70, then $140. Limit: users are capped at one, three and five by plan.

Photos matter in concrete because the work gets buried. They also settle disputes about thickness and base depth. Shoot the base, forms, rebar and vapor barrier before every pour. If a crack claim arrives a year later, those photos show what was under the slab.

Which tools bring in concrete bid requests?

Software runs the job, but bid requests come from search, maps and ads. Google states that creating a Business Profile is free, so a complete profile is the cheapest lead tool you can own.

Limit: a profile needs photos of finished work and replies to every review.

Paid search suits concrete well because homeowners search at the moment they decide. See the pricing page for every plan.

How do you move one concrete job from bid to final invoice?

Run every job through the same five steps, and make each tool own one step. That keeps data from living in three places.

  • Measure: takeoff in STACK or your estimating tool, with thickness, rebar and finish noted.
  • Bid: send the proposal and collect a deposit before you order material.
  • Schedule: book forming, pour and finishing as separate stops, with a weather backup date.
  • Document: take photos at base, rebar and finish.
  • Bill: invoice from the signed bid so change orders show as line items.

If your tools do not pass data between steps, choose the step you lose money on and fix that first. Most concrete firms lose it at the bid, where one wrong yard count or missed pump fee cuts the margin.

How do you choose concrete contractor software for your company?

Choose concrete contractor software with a three-check filter: fit, cost and setup effort. Run every tool through all three before you pay.

Fit: does it measure from plans or photos, price by the yard and square foot, and handle change orders?

Cost: add the plan, per-user fees, job caps and card fees, then compare the total with the margin on one average pour.

Setup effort: can an estimator load a price list and three saved templates in one week?

Company typeStarting stackAdd next
Owner and one crew, flatworkJoist Pro, QuickBooks Simple Start, free Business ProfileServiceM8 Free or Starter
Two to five crews, mixed workSTACK takeoff, ServiceM8 Growing or Jobber, QuickBooks EssentialsCompanyCam
Foundations and commercial bidsJobTread or Contractor Foreman Plus, STACK, QuickBooks PlusMarketing support for lead flow

A one-crew shop should keep the stack short. A multi-crew company that bids commercial work should test the cost tracking against a finished job before moving all active jobs over.

Software does not create demand. For fast sign-offs and photos of finished slabs, a website with a project gallery helps bids convert.

What should a concrete bid template include?

A bid template is the cheapest software upgrade a concrete company can make. Build it once in your estimating tool, then reuse it so every bid carries the same checks.

  • Quantities: square feet, thickness, cubic yards with a waste allowance, and linear feet of forms.
  • Reinforcement: rebar or mesh by size and spacing, plus chairs and tie wire.
  • Site work: excavation, base rock, compaction and haul-off, each as its own line.
  • Finishing: broom, stamped, colored or exposed aggregate, priced per square foot.
  • Extras: pump truck, saw cuts, sealer and a weather delay allowance.
  • Terms: deposit, payment schedule, and how change orders are priced.

Review the template after every lost bid and every job that ran over. Write down which line was wrong and why. If the same line keeps moving, the template has a gap. That feedback loop is worth more than any extra feature.

What do concrete contractors get wrong when they buy software?

The first error is paying per user for people who only need to look. Check whether crew leads, subs and clients can view a job for free before you count seats. JobTread lists free vendor and customer portal users, for example.

The second error is trusting a headline price. Contractor Foreman shows a $49 headline that applies to one plan on annual billing only. STACK shows prices as low as. Read the billing terms before you compare.

The third error is skipping the pilot. Run one live job through the tool, from takeoff to invoice, before you move the whole company. A pilot costs a few days and shows the gaps a demo hides. Ask the crew lead who used it what slowed the day down.

What software does a concrete contractor need?

A concrete contractor needs a way to measure and bid work, schedule pours, document jobs and take payment. Start with an estimate tool and a free Google Business Profile. Add a takeoff tool when bids increase, and project cost software when change orders start slipping through.

How much does concrete contractor software cost?

Published prices in this guide start at $0 for ServiceM8 Free and $10 a month for Joist Basics. Jobber Core is $29 to $49 a month, and Contractor Foreman Plus is $199 on monthly billing. STACK lists takeoff from $299 per user monthly. Card fees and extra users cost more.

Is there free takeoff software for concrete?

STACK states that its Takeoff and Estimate product has a free version. The page does not list the limits of that free version, so test it on a real plan set before you rely on it. Paid takeoff plans are listed from $299 per user per month.

Can Jobber run a concrete contracting business?

Jobber handles scheduling, quotes, invoices and payments, so it suits small flatwork crews. Core is $49 a month with no commitment or $29 billed annually for one user. It is not a takeoff tool, so pair it with a measuring method for large bids.

Do concrete contractors need a website if they use bid software?

Yes. Bid software runs the work after a request arrives, but it does not bring requests in. A website with pages for driveways, patios and foundations, plus a project gallery and a Google Business Profile, gives owners a reason to call you.

What is the difference between JobTread and Contractor Foreman?

Both cover estimates, budgets and change orders. JobTread lists one plan at $199 a month plus $20 per extra user on monthly billing. Contractor Foreman lists tiers by user count, with Plus at $199 for up to eight users monthly. Compare them on one real job.

What should a new concrete crew buy first?

Set up a free Google Business Profile and an estimate app first. Joist Basics at $10 a month or ServiceM8 Free are cheap starts. Add takeoff and project cost tools only when bid volume or change orders start costing you real margin.

Both cover estimates, budgets and change orders. JobTread lists one plan at $199 a month plus $20 per extra user on monthly billing. Contractor Foreman lists tiers by user count, with Plus at $199 for up to eight users monthly. Compare them on one real job.
###
What should a new concrete crew buy first?
Set up a free Google Business Profile and an estimate app first. Joist Basics at $10 a month or ServiceM8 Free are cheap starts. Add takeoff and project cost tools only when bid volume or change orders start costing you real margin.
